teaser: VoiceDebrief runs with no server on the user's own key; the one thing it cannot sell is a capped key, and this maps who could allow it and what to ask them.
core_idea: VoiceDebrief turns a voice note into a transcript and a debrief in the browser on the user's own key, with no server by design, and its commercial model was never a billing system: a user pays once, we keep our cut, the rest becomes the credit limit on a key we hand over and the provider meters; OpenRouter's Management API describes that mechanism and its terms forbid reselling access, which is where the project's commit history stops, the same shape as Apple's licence stopping a Mac leased by the minute; the map of every provider's terms and docs shows only OpenRouter and ElevenLabs have keys that carry a ceiling, ElevenLabs has OEM terms and a grants programme, four routes remain, and the brief asks every provider the same sentence: let the credit limit be a property of a key a user can buy.

nodes.label: VoiceDebrief
nodes.summary: One pass in the browser on the user's own OpenRouter key: transcript, translation, debrief, infographic; no account, no server, nothing stored.

nodes.label: The handbrake in the commit history
nodes.summary: 239 commits and 27 releases in three weeks of August 2026, then eleven, then three; the stop is the commercial model, not the code.

nodes.label: No server is the product
nodes.summary: Never seeing the audio removes custody, governance, breach, key management, billing, scaling and on-call at once; a server brings all of it back at once.

nodes.label: The model is a property of the key
nodes.summary: A user pays once, we keep our share at that moment, the rest is the credit limit on a key they hold, the provider meters; billing by not building billing.

nodes.label: Described in the docs, forbidden by the terms
nodes.summary: OpenRouter's Management API creates capped keys for each customer instance; section 7(4) of its terms forbids reselling API access to models.

nodes.label: The same shape as Agent Desk
nodes.summary: The product is possible and the licence is the blocker, as with Apple's rule against leasing a Mac for less than a day.

nodes.label: The provider map
nodes.summary: From each provider's own pages: whether one key can carry a ceiling and whether it may be handed to a paying user; only OpenRouter and ElevenLabs cap a key.

nodes.label: ElevenLabs, the nearest fit
nodes.summary: Per-key credit limits, OEM terms for making the service available to end users at the customer's own price, Scribe at $0.22 an hour, a twelve-month grants programme.

nodes.label: Four routes
nodes.summary: The forbidden one; a provider that sells or permits the capped key; bring your own key, kept; a metering proxy, which is the backend the product exists to avoid.

nodes.label: The one-sentence ask
nodes.summary: Let the credit limit be a property of a key that a user can buy through us, so that we never hold the audio and never run the meter; a brief per provider for the agents.

quotes.text: What stopped it was not a server. It was the lack of one.
The two providers whose keys carry a ceiling, OpenRouter and ElevenLabs, are the two whose terms say the most about resale, because a capped key is the thing that makes resale easy.
let the credit limit be a property of a key that a user can buy through us, so that we never hold the audio and never run the meter.

figures.caption: What each provider's terms and docs say, in October 2026, about a capped key in a user's hand, and the four routes: the one that was planned and forbidden, the one to ask for, the one that runs today, and the backend the product was built to avoid.
voicedebrief.ai on 12 October 2026. One recording in, four artefacts out, in the browser, on the user's own key; the maximum a pass can cost is quoted before it starts.

The page that gets a user from nothing to a working key, and its one instruction in bold: set a credit limit on the key, because a key with a limit cannot cost you more than the limit. The ceiling is the user's, not ours.
